summary.text: Influenza A virus, or IAV, is a pathogen whose strains cause seasonal flu in humans and can also infect birds and some mammals.
Its subtypes are defined by the combination of two surface proteins, hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N), as in H1N1.
The virus changes through mutation and genetic reassortment, which lets it evade immunity and sometimes jump between species.

paragraphs.heading: A virus of people, birds and beasts
paragraphs.text: Influenza A virus, often shortened to IAV, is the germ behind the flu that comes round every season in people. It does not stay with humans alone. Some strains live in birds, and others keep circulating among bats, pigs, horses and dogs, while further mammals catch it now and then. IAV has also set off several pandemics, the best known being the Spanish Flu of 1918 to 1920.

paragraphs.heading: Names built from two proteins
paragraphs.text: Two proteins stick out from the virus's outer coat: hemagglutinin, written H, and neuraminidase, written N. Both are antigenic, meaning a host's immune system can recognise them and make antibodies against them. Each subtype of the virus is named after the pair it carries, so H5N1 has hemagglutinin of type 5 and neuraminidase of type 1. There are 18 known kinds of H and 11 kinds of N. Wild birds have yielded almost every pairing of H1 to H16 with N1 to N11, while H17 and H18 have turned up only in bats.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the particle
paragraphs.text: A single virus particle, called a virion, measures 80 to 120 nanometres across; the smaller ones are oval and the larger ones are long threads. Its genes are written in RNA, split into eight separate pieces called segments. A protein named NP wraps each piece into a spiral, and three larger proteins, PB1, PB2 and PA, sit on every segment to copy and read the RNA. A layer of the M1 protein surrounds this core, and outside that lies an envelope of fatty membrane taken from the host cell.

paragraphs.heading: Why the flu keeps changing
paragraphs.text: The virus keeps changing, through mutation and through what is called genetic reassortment. These changes help it slip past immunity and sometimes leap from one species to another. Small differences inside a subtype can change how readily it spreads, how ill it makes people, and which hosts it can infect. That is why flu vaccines have to be reworked again and again to keep pace with the virus.

paragraphs.heading: Illness in people and poultry
paragraphs.text: Seasonal flu in people usually brings fever, cough, sore throat, aching muscles and headache, and in bad cases breathing trouble and a pneumonia that can kill. Now and then a person catches a bird or pig strain, most often after close contact with sick animals, and the illness can range from mild to deadly. In some water birds a bird strain causes no signs at all, yet the same strain can be lethal once it reaches chickens. Poultry can be vaccinated against it, though quarantine, keeping flocks apart and good hygiene are the favoured defences.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping watch worldwide
paragraphs.text: In people, a vaccine can prevent seasonal flu, and antiviral medicines can treat it if given early. A worldwide network called the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System, or GISRS, tracks how flu spreads and guides the making of vaccines for both ordinary seasons and pandemics. Its laboratories in 127 countries test several million samples every year. They watch not only human viruses but also bird, pig and other flu viruses that might one day infect people.
